posts.title: LinkedIn intake — NVIDIA PAIR personal AI cluster
posts.headline: 🚀 NVIDIA PAIR can discover the computers on your network and route inference across them.
posts.author: Javier Medel, MSc
posts.post_text:
🚀 NVIDIA PAIR can discover the computers on your network and route inference across them. ⚡🧠

This one caught my attention.

Your RTX gaming PC.
Your AI workstation.
Your Mac.
Your NVIDIA DGX Spark.

Instead of treating them as separate machines, PAIR can turn them into a personal AI inference cluster.

And the crazy part?

You don't need racks, special cables, or complicated cluster orchestration.

PAIR can:

🧠 Discover available local compute
⚡ Route workloads where capacity is available
🔀 Run agent tasks in parallel
🔒 Keep prompts, files & context on your network
🛠️ Work with Ollama + LM Studio
💻 Connect Windows, Linux & macOS

I think this gets especially interesting with agentic AI.

Why have 10 tasks fighting over one GPU when you can spread them across machines that are already sitting idle?

You might not need a $20K AI server.

You might already own the compute.

Stop thinking about your AI PC.

Start thinking about your AI network. 🤯
posts.summary_html:
Post summary

The post presents NVIDIA PAIR as a way to discover local machines and route AI inference among them rather than treating a gaming PC, workstation, Mac, or DGX Spark as isolated resources. It claims a personal AI cluster can distribute agent work across spare local capacity, retain prompts, files, and context on the local network, and work with Ollama and LM Studio across Windows, Linux, and macOS.

Book relevance

Candidate chapters: local AI infrastructure; agent orchestration and capacity planning; private inference boundaries; operational reliability of multi-machine systems.

Candidate claim/example: A local agent system can treat nearby heterogeneous machines as a capacity pool, but a useful routing layer must make hardware eligibility, local-network trust, model/runtime compatibility, task placement, and failure handling explicit rather than merely advertising unused compute.

Hermione relevance

Moderate relevance. Hermione could use a verified local-capacity inventory and a bounded scheduler for suitable background workloads, instead of assuming one GPU or host. Any adoption would require explicit device authorization, authenticated/segmented local networking, resource quotas, workload-data classification, compatibility tests, observability, and graceful fallbacks. NVIDIA's beta documentation is not sufficient proof that the product meets Hermione's safety or reliability needs.

Evidence and limitations

Evidence strength: moderate for the existence and content of the LinkedIn post, the publicly documented NVIDIA PAIR beta, its stated compatible-device categories, its advertised local endpoint, and launch support for Ollama and LM Studio; discovery-only for performance, real task parallelism, privacy/security guarantees, cost savings, cross-platform reliability, and suitability for a particular network.

The LinkedIn post is social/discovery evidence. NVIDIA's product page is a vendor primary source, not an independent evaluation. Its claims about keeping data local and distributing requests need confirmation against installation documentation, network traffic, authentication and authorization behavior, supported model/runtime combinations, telemetry, fault recovery, and measured workload tests. No software was downloaded, installed, configured, or run.

posts.title: LinkedIn intake — Hardware-aware local LLM selection with llmfit
posts.headline: Stop guessing which AI model your computer can actually handle 🔥
posts.author: Kushal Banda
posts.post_text:
Stop guessing which AI model your computer can actually handle 🔥

There's an open-source tool called llmfit that looks at your hardware and tells you which LLMs you can realistically run locally. It's already picked up 35K+ GitHub stars.

Instead of downloading a huge model and hoping for the best, llmfit checks your:
• RAM
• CPU
• GPU
• VRAM

Then it compares hundreds of models across four things that actually matter:

• Compatibility - whether the model will fit
• Performance - estimated tokens per second
• Quality - based on model size and quantization
• Context - the context window your machine can support

It'll also auto-pick the best quantization level for your setup, tuning it until it finds something your hardware can actually run.

One feature I really like: it understands Mixture-of-Experts models properly. Take Mixtral 8x7B, it has 46.7B total parameters, but only ~12.9B get activated per token. Most tools would just treat it like a 46.7B model. llmfit accounts for the difference when estimating performance.

It covers models from Meta, Mistral, Qwen, DeepSeek, and more, and plugs into:

• Ollama
• llama.cpp
• MLX
• LM Studio

Fully open source, MIT licensed.

Would this change how you pick your next local model? Curious if others have run into the "downloaded a model that was too big" problem too.

Link in the comments 👇

#AI #LLM #OpenSource #LocalAI
posts.summary_html:
Post summary

The post introduces llmfit as an open-source hardware-aware model-selection tool. It says the tool inspects RAM, CPU, GPU, and VRAM, then ranks local LLM options by compatibility, estimated tokens per second, quality, and supported context. It also claims dynamic quantization choice and MoE-aware estimates, using Mixtral 8x7B as an example where active parameters differ from total parameters.

Book relevance

Candidate chapters: local AI infrastructure and hardware planning; model evaluation and deployment fit; LLMOps performance estimation; memory hierarchy and Mixture-of-Experts trade-offs.

Candidate claim/example: Local-model selection should be a compatibility-and-measurement workflow, not a parameter-count comparison. Estimate memory, context, runtime backend, and likely generation speed first; then validate the shortlisted model with a representative local benchmark before treating it as operationally suitable.

Hermione relevance

Moderate relevance. Hermione can use a hardware-aware, read-only planning step before attempting local/offline inference or allocating models to specialist workflows. This is most useful for private or slow background work. It is not a drop-in basis for interactive assistant serving: model quality, token latency, startup/download time, context needs, provider compatibility, security posture, and measured reliability still need workload-specific validation.

Evidence and limitations

Evidence strength: moderate for the existence of the public LinkedIn post, the guest-visible comment, the inspected public llmfit repository, its MIT license, its documented hardware/model-fit features, and its implementation of explicit estimated-versus-measured confidence states at the inspected commit; discovery-only for the post’s popularity figure, generalized accuracy of any recommendation, dynamic quantization quality, cross-provider behavior, and claimed performance on a particular machine.

The LinkedIn material remains social/discovery evidence. The repository README and source code document intended functionality, including hardware detection, fit scoring, estimate basis/confidence, local and community benchmark support, and optional runtime-provider actions. They do not independently prove model compatibility, tokens-per-second accuracy, safe download/provider behavior, or production fitness on Hermione’s hardware. No package was installed, no models were downloaded, and no benchmark or provider integration was run during this intake.

posts.title: LinkedIn intake — LLM inference: prefill/decode and system trade-offs
posts.headline: I was reading about inference from this article by Byte Byte Go, and one idea reframed how I think about LLM latency.
posts.author: Hrushik Pabbathi
posts.post_text:
I was reading about inference from this article by Byte Byte Go, and one idea reframed how I think about LLM latency.

Every time a model responds, two very different operations run back to back on the same GPU.

Prefill: reads your whole prompt at once, spits out the first token. Compute-bound; more raw GPU power directly helps.

Decode: generates every token after that, one at a time, each depending on the last. Memory-bandwidth-bound; the GPU is mostly waiting on weights to load, not crunching numbers.
Opposite bottlenecks. Which means almost every optimization technique in production AI exists because of this split.

A few that stood out:
→ Batching: stack multiple users' requests together so the GPU stays busy. Great for throughput, worse for any single user's latency.
→ Prefix caching: reuse computation for repeated prompt prefixes (like a shared system prompt). Only works if the very first tokens match exactly.
→ Quantization: shrink weight precision (16-bit → 8-bit/4-bit) to speed up both phases, ~30-50% gains, but attention layers are the most fragile and usually get left at full precision.
→ Speculative decoding: a small draft model guesses several tokens ahead, the big model just verifies them in one pass instead of generating one at a time.
→ Disaggregation: split prefill and decode across entirely different GPUs, ship the cache between them. Most architectural of the bunch.
Also a good reality check: most teams should start on off-the-shelf APIs, not a custom inference stack. The switch usually makes sense once API costs, latency needs, or reliability requirements genuinely outgrow what a vendor can offer, not before.

Full article here: https://lnkd.in/dbkmPfHn


#AI #MachineLearning #LLM #InferenceEngineering #GPU #AIInfrastructure #DeepLearning #MLOps #GenerativeAI #SoftwareEngineering
posts.summary_html:
Post summary

The post explains LLM serving through two phases: prefill processes the prompt and produces the first token plus KV cache, while decode generates later tokens serially. It frames prefill as compute-bound and decode as memory-bandwidth-bound, then introduces batching, exact-prefix KV-cache reuse, quantization, speculative decoding, and prefill/decode disaggregation as techniques with different throughput and latency trade-offs. It recommends starting with managed APIs until measured cost, latency, or reliability needs justify operating a custom serving stack.

Book relevance

Candidate chapters: LLMOps and inference economics; agent latency and reliability; context engineering and cache-aware prompts; build-versus-buy infrastructure decisions.

Candidate claim/example: Agent cost and responsiveness are jointly shaped by serving-layer mechanics. Separate TTFT, decode tokens/second, queueing, cache hit rate, and tail latency; optimize only against representative workloads, and use cache reuse only with clear data scope and invalidation rules.

Hermione relevance

High relevance. Hermione uses repeated system, tool, and workflow context, so a self-hosted serving path could benefit from compatible prefix/KV reuse. The operational lesson is not to turn caching on indiscriminately: isolate cache state by user/session/tenant and model version, keep variable or sensitive material out of shared prefixes where appropriate, monitor hit rate and P95 latency, and validate that a managed API is not the simpler and safer choice.

Evidence and limitations

Evidence strength: moderate for the public post, its explanatory image, the ByteByteGo explanation of the prefill/decode distinction, and vLLM's documented automatic prefix caching; discovery-only for the post's stated 30–50% quantization gain, generalized GPU characterization, the custom-stack decision threshold, and performance/cost effects in any particular deployment.

LinkedIn material remains social/discovery evidence. The captured post provides no workload, model, hardware, concurrency, TTFT/TPS/P95 measurements, quality evaluation, cost model, cache-isolation design, or independent benchmark. The external ByteByteGo article link was resolved and fetched by a normal network request from captured post metadata, not clicked through LinkedIn. Its explanation is useful context but is not a reproducible benchmark or a deployment recommendation.

posts.title: LinkedIn intake — semantic boundaries for multi-agent systems
posts.headline: I have spent the last few months building multi-agent systems.
posts.author: Tony Seale
posts.post_text:
I have spent the last few months building multi-agent systems. Building them, running them, watching them talk.

And it is becoming clear where this is heading.

OpenClaw 2.0 shipped this week with a move towards collaborative agents. Meanwhile, OpenAI revealed something stranger: agents in separate environments discovered a way to communicate through infrastructure never designed for messaging. Hundreds of them then used it to coordinate the attack on Hugging Face.

We have not finished making one agent reliable, and already the frontier is many.

Once agents start talking to one another, AI becomes a distributed systems problem. And that is what the Semantic Web was designed for.

🔵 The Information Boundary Matters

The moment two agents communicate, something crosses between them.

Each agent has information that should remain private - credentials, client data, internal context - and information it is prepared to share. The hard part is that the useful and the private are tangled together.

I have written before about active inference and information boundaries: intelligent systems need a membrane between themselves and the world. Multi-agent systems make that concrete. Every agent has a boundary, and you have to decide what crosses it. DPROD 1.2 will add ODRL-based data contracts that can scale to this complexity.

🔵 English Is Not Enough

Agents can talk in natural language. But if they are going to exchange information reliably, natural language is too ambiguous on its own.

“The customer.” “The contract.” “The product.”

Two agents can use the same words while meaning different things.

We tighten that in two ways.

First, shared concepts. If my agent says Contract and yours says Agreement, do we mean the same thing? Connecting agents starts to look like ontology alignment - a negotiation about how their models of the world correspond.

Second, shared identifiers. Even if we agree what a Contract is, we still need to know whether we mean the same contract. You need an identifier both sides can resolve. In a distributed system, the obvious pattern is the one the Web already gave us: a URL.

🔵 Semantics Is Compression

Agents are chatty. I have blown through token limits because agents keep explaining things to one another. Semantics is not only about precision. It is also about compression. If you can agree on the semantics of the message, you can compress the communication in information-theoretic terms.

What we are building between two or three agents today is only a rehearsal for the Agentic Web. Ontologies and URLs were designed to let independently built systems exchange meaning across boundaries at global scale. We are rediscovering it one agent at a time.

⭕ Sharing: https://lnkd.in/eAr-iD-b
⭕ Boundary: https://lnkd.in/er_HjtWg
🔗 KGG: https://lnkd.in/eSrYRybk
posts.summary_html:
Post summary

The post frames multi-agent coordination as a distributed-systems problem. It argues that each agent needs an information boundary, that natural-language exchange alone is too ambiguous, and that shared concepts plus resolvable identifiers can make cross-agent exchange more precise and less token-heavy. It presents ontologies and URLs as a basis for shared meaning and identity.

Book relevance

High relevance for chapters on multi-agent architecture, context engineering, semantic interoperability, information boundaries, provenance, and governed delegation.

Candidate claim/example: Multi-agent systems need explicit, machine-readable contracts for the meaning, identity, authority, provenance, and permitted disclosure of exchanged objects. Shared terminology alone is not a security boundary; it must be paired with least-privilege access, data minimization, policy enforcement, and testable outcomes.

Hermione relevance

High relevance. Hermione already coordinates specialized workers, queues, archives, and tool scopes. The item supports using canonical task and artifact identifiers, typed hand-off records, explicit permitted fields, per-worker authority boundaries, and durable provenance. It does not justify broad sharing of memory or credentials: worker-to-worker exchange should be minimized, scoped, auditable, and independently verified.

Evidence and limitations

Evidence strength: moderate for the existence of the public post, its stated architecture perspective, the captured image, and the visible discussion; discovery-only for claims about OpenClaw releases, OpenAI-disclosed agent coordination, attacks, DPROD 1.2, or real-world security/cost benefits.

The LinkedIn post and comments are social/discovery evidence, not proof that ontology alignment or URLs alone produce reliable, secure multi-agent behavior. The post provides no system design, repository, controlled evaluation, authorization model, privacy analysis, protocol trace, cost data, or independent security assessment. Any cross-agent design should be evaluated for channel-bound identity, explicit authorization and revocation, constrained disclosure, replay/loop handling, quotas, audit evidence, and measurable task outcomes.

posts.title: LinkedIn intake — GPT-6 Astra, long-context evaluation, and security implications
posts.headline: I kveld har OpenAI lansert GPT-6 Astra og mange bommer på de viktigste detaljene...
posts.author: Marius Sandbu
posts.post_text:
I kveld har OpenAI lansert GPT-6 Astra og mange bommer på de viktigste detaljene...

Context is king!

Alle, absolutt ALLE språkmodeller sliter med tap av kontekst og hallusinering når det blir for mye informasjon, f.eks < 200,000 tokens (150,000 ord). Det fylles fort opp når man har flere virtuelle agenter eller store mengder data.

Derfor er disse målingene/testene viktige:

MRCRv2 tester om modellen finner og bruker riktig informasjon i enorme mengder tekst.
AA-Omniscience tester om modellen vet hva den ikke vet, eller bare finner på et svar.

På MRCRv2:
256K–512K tokens: fra 91,5 % (GPT 5.6 Sol) til 100 % (Astra)
512K–1M tokens: fra 73,8 %(GPT 5.6 Sol) til 96,3 % (Astra)

Hallusinering faller også fra 12,2 % til 4,2 % (Fra en brukertest)
AA-Omniscience fra  22 poeng (GPT 5.6 Sol) til 44 poeng (Astra)

Andre tester også har det blitt en del store løft.

OSWorld 2.0 tester praktiske oppgaver interaktivt på en datamaskin: ca. 40 minutter, mot 75 min (GPT 5.6 Sol)
ARC-AGI-3 tester evnen til å forstå og løse helt nye problemer: 99,9 % (Astra), mot 7,8 % (GPT 5.6 Sol)
ExploitBench tester om kjente sårbarheter kan gjøres om til fungerende exploits: 100 % (Astra) mot 78,5 % (GPT 5.6 Sol)
SRE-Bench tester reverse engineering av programvare uten kildekode: 88 % (Astra) mot 55,9 % (GPT 5.6 Sol)

Som med Mythos og andre nye frontier språkmodeller,  vil også dette påvirke IT-sikkerhet mer fremover.
Vi får modeller som raskere kan finne sårbarheter, analysere skadevare og forstå komplekse systemer. Fantastisk for oss som jobber med IT-sikkerhet samt analyse, men minst like verdifullt for angriperne...

Det viktigste med Astra-lanseringen er ikke bare at modellen «tenker bedre».
Den husker mer, mister mindre kontekst og klarer faktisk å bruke informasjonen bedre. Det vil selvsagt påvirke absolutt alle bruksområder (å samtidig at den "sløser" mindre tokens)
posts.summary_html:
Book relevance

High relevance for chapters on context engineering, agent-memory limits, evaluation, LLM operations, security capability shifts, and multi-agent cost controls.

Candidate claim/example: Long-context agent quality should be evaluated through retrieval/use of relevant evidence, calibrated abstention, realistic task completion, cost, and safety—not context-window size or vendor headline scores alone.

Hermione relevance

High relevance. Hermione uses lengthy system instructions, tools, queues, archives, and multi-step workflows. The item reinforces the value of concise task state, retrieval with provenance, explicit uncertainty, bounded history, cache/retention policies, and independent success checks. Any use of a large-context model should be benchmarked against Hermione’s own workload for accuracy, latency, spend, sensitive-context isolation, and security behavior before relying on vendor or social claims.

Evidence strength and limitations

Evidence strength: moderate for the documented GPT-6 Astra model identity, context window, and listed API prices; discovery-only for the LinkedIn author’s benchmark and security-effect claims.

The primary post is a social-media source. Visible engagement and comments are a time-bound partial snapshot; collapsed or hidden replies were not opened. The post supplies no linked benchmark methodology, hardware, sampling protocol, model settings, confidence intervals, or independent replication. Greater capability on reverse-engineering or exploit-oriented benchmarks is dual-use and should be assessed through authorization, task scoping, environment isolation, credential/egress controls, logging, and human approval rather than inferred from a score alone.

posts.title: LinkedIn intake: JIT-Agent and task-specific agent harnesses
posts.headline: Self-evolving agent harnesses are here.
posts.author: Akshay Pachaar
posts.post_text:
Self-evolving agent harnesses are here.

(100% open-source)

Today you pick a fixed harness, and every task runs through it. A deep research question and a file-renaming task get the same memory strategy, the same planner, and the same tools exposed at every step.

JIT-Agent is a 27B open-source model that writes the harness instead. You hand it the task and the tool registry, and it emits four Python files plus a prompt config.

That happens once, before the task starts. Then a second model, one you don't train or modify, does the actual work by being called step by step from inside those files. It never writes any of the code and never sees it.

Each file covers one part of a fixed four-module contract:

→ Memory decides what slice of the history that second model sees at the current step.
→ Planning turns that view into a directive for the next action.
→ Tool policy decides which tools are exposed for that directive.
→ Action assembles the prompt from all of it, calls the model, and interprets the reply as either a tool call to run or a final answer.

Because the code is written per task, the same generator produces structurally different agents.

Here are a few tasks from the JIT-Agent paper, and the harness each one produced:

1) For a request that had to find contact records, build a workbook, and email it, it compiled the requirements into a dependency graph where delivery waits on artifact verification, and stored intermediate artifacts so later nodes consume finished results instead of rebuilding them from the transcript.

2) For a multi-hop identity question, a fixed graph would commit too early to one evidence path, so it synthesized a delegate tool that opens a private research subagent with its own memory and a five-step budget. The returned answer re-enters the parent loop as an ordinary observation.

3) For a task built around comparing numbers and ranking the results, it kept the arithmetic out of the model. The harness computes the numbers by running code, stores the results as fixed values, and hands those same values to every later step, so the model reads figures instead of recomputing them from text.

Holding the working model fixed and changing only the harness, JIT-Agent's harnesses matched or beat hand-built runtimes on search and instruction benchmarks while spending well under half the tokens, and roughly a third less per case on average. Writing the harness costs tokens too, and that cost sits outside those per-case numbers.

So harness design stops being one choice you commit to and becomes something written fresh for each task. JIT-Agent also keeps the harnesses that beat its current best in an archive, and pulls from it when a later task looks similar. Its own weights never change while this happens.

This work is fully open-source.

Link to the paper and the GitHub repo in the first comment.
posts.summary_html:
Book relevance

Score: 9/10 — candidate chapters: agent orchestration and harness engineering; task-adaptive state and tool policy; evaluation, cost accounting, and verifiable autonomy.

The durable lesson is not that a generated harness is automatically better. It is that a task-specific harness can make memory scope, plan structure, tool exposure, deterministic computation, delegation, artifact checkpoints, and final verification explicit executable choices. Claims of a cheaper or stronger agent must include generator cost, execution cost, completion rate, latency, retries, verifier/judge behavior, and comparable real-workload evaluation.

Hermione relevance

Score: 9/10. Hermione already uses isolated workers, scoped tool access, durable queue checkpoints, explicit verification, and an execution boundary. This item supports making those controls task-specific only where they remain inspectable and governed: self-contained worker briefs, narrow capability grants, hard token/time/retry budgets, immutable artifact checkpoints, independent acceptance checks, and safe fallback/stop behavior. Generated harness code must be reviewed and sandboxed before it receives credentials or effectful tools; a model-generated policy is not a security boundary.

Evidence assessment and next action

Evidence is moderate for the repository- and paper-documented architecture, and discovery-only for broad effectiveness, cost, and benchmark-comparison claims. The repository and arXiv preprint were inspected directly by network fetch, not through LinkedIn. No installation, credentials, model serving, or generated-harness execution was performed. See wider-web-research.md for the pinned primary-source review.

posts.title: Agent sandboxing needs a real boundary plus explicit network and credential controls
posts.headline: ArcBox: agent sandboxes need isolation plus explicit egress and credential controls
posts.author: André Lindenberg
posts.post_text:
Clicking Allow on every agent command was never security, it was a reflex. ArcBox removes the click. Running abctl claude boots Claude Code into its own Firecracker microVM, own kernel, empty disk, nothing mounted from the host, only what the agent clones itself. The same daemon also runs Docker and full Linux VMs on your Mac. 2.9k stars, Apache-2.0.
#AIAgents #RuntimeSecurity #AgentInfra #Rust #OpenSource
posts.summary_html:
Post summary

André Lindenberg presents ArcBox as a local macOS runtime for containers and virtual machines. The post says that abctl claude starts Claude Code in a Firecracker microVM with its own kernel and empty disk rather than relying on per-command permission prompts. It also claims Docker and full Linux VM support, roughly 2.9k GitHub stars, and Apache-2.0 licensing.

Primary-source quick pass

The GitHub repository named in a captured visible author comment was inspected directly by ordinary network fetch, not by clicking it in LinkedIn. At observed commit 55b384b9193d9e564b33efe208dcc7ad5d63b0ff, its README and sandbox docs describe disposable Firecracker microVMs, an empty /workspace with no host mounts, a non-root Claude session, and session-only forwarding limited to selected Anthropic/Claude environment variables. The API documentation makes network enabled the default and exposes an explicit NETWORK_MODE_NONE; it describes TTL and idle cleanup, lifecycle events, checkpoints, restore, and resource release. The inspected source tree contains a host-socket egress component, but this pass did not establish an allowlist/default-deny egress policy or independently audit the enforcement boundary.

Book relevance

  • Candidate chapters: agent runtime security; tool execution and approval boundaries; credential isolation and egress governance; durable state, cleanup, and recovery.
  • Candidate claim: permission prompts are not a sufficient primary security boundary for autonomous code; a usable runtime needs a meaningful isolation boundary, disposable or revertible state, explicit network policy, scoped credentials, limits, and auditable lifecycle.
  • Candidate example: ArcBox documents an empty-workspace microVM workflow for a coding agent, plus TTL/idle cleanup and checkpoint/restore semantics.
  • Counterweight: a microVM alone does not prove safe egress, secret handling, host-integration security, sandbox-escape resistance, or production effectiveness.

Hermione relevance

This is directly relevant to Hermione because she can operate shells, browsers, repositories, and networked tools on content-derived tasks. It supports preserving the existing separation between read-only research and explicit side effects, and it adds a concrete runtime checklist: no dangerous host mounts or Docker socket, network disabled or externally allowlisted when unneeded, short-lived scoped credentials kept outside prompts/logs, hard resource/time limits, and reviewable cleanup/recovery evidence. ArcBox is macOS-oriented and its documented sandbox prerequisites do not make it a drop-in replacement for Hermione's Linux environment.

Evidence and limitations

Evidence strength: moderate for the repository's documented architecture and API defaults at the observed commit; discovery-only for the LinkedIn claims' security, sub-100 ms boot, ease of operation, compatibility, and real-world outcomes.

  • The submitted lnkd.in URL resolved non-interactively to a referral-bearing LinkedIn share route. Guest-visible canonical metadata established activity 7501324957306593280; the intermediate share-route number and referral parameters were excluded from committed metadata.
  • The authenticated visible target-post viewport showed André Lindenberg's post, image, and multiple comments with no login wall, MFA, CAPTCHA, or security checkpoint. No LinkedIn controls or links were clicked. The raw full-screen capture remains local-only because it includes unrelated LinkedIn UI.
  • Four guest-visible comments were archived while LinkedIn reported five comments. One author comment supplied the public ArcBox repository; a visible reply usefully asks whether egress is empty by default. Replies, sorting, expansion, and later comments were not opened, so coverage is partial.
  • The source documentation says a sandbox's default network mode is enabled. The repository's userspace/host-socket networking code supports a concrete implementation path, but this read-only pass did not verify policy enforcement outside a potentially privileged guest, audit escape paths, or test whether package installation/network access is default-deny.
  • No package, binary, virtual machine, sandbox, credential, benchmark, security audit, CVE review, or independent escape test was run. The repository's security policy defines a reporting process and scope, not independent assurance.

Media summary

One static author-provided image was archived as media/image-1.jpg. It shows an ArcBox README-style view with a project card saying it runs AI agents on isolated machines with their own kernel, filesystem, and network and a sub-100 ms boot claim. It is project material that illustrates the claim, not independent proof.

posts.title: Desktop governance needs enforceable policy boundaries, not just configuration inventory
posts.headline: Agentdesktop: open-source governance for AI tools on desktop fleets
posts.author: Christian Posta
posts.post_text:
🗣️  🎉  🙌 We are super excited to announce a new open-source project: 𝐀𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐝𝐞𝐬𝐤𝐭𝐨𝐩! Let's get the same powerful AI governance, observability, and security that we have in server environments out to our desktops and workstations.

 👉 Every organization is dealing with AI tooling sprawl (agents, harneses, MCP servers, skills, etc). MDM solves half of the battle: device enrollment, deploying software, OS patching etc. While it *can* deploy custom scripts, etc it's a leaky proposition: what starts off as "simple quick scripts" quickly becomes a full-blown integration nightmare trying to keep track of all different tools, different configuration formats/files, across multiple operating systems, scraping MCP servers/skills (without exposing sensitive credentials), etc.

 ⚠️ And all these AI tools seem to LOVE API keys and secrets. And this proliferates runtime credential sprawl. A leaked credential remains useful independently of the user or device it was originally running on.

 ✅ We think Agentdesktop can help with this problem:

▫️ AI tool/harness discovery and inventory: detect AI tools, MCP servers, skills and models
▫️ Tool-native config management: centrally manage, version, and reconcile native settings for tools such as Claude Code, Codex, VS Code, and others
▫️ Harness-native sandbox policy: define filesystem and network restrictions once, then translate them into each supported harness’s native sandbox configuration
▫️ User and device identity: Device key/certs, bound to user identity/SSO, bound to AI agents
▫️ Runtime credentials: short lived, tool-specific credentials; provider API keys/sensitive credentials can be injected transparently at the gateway instead of being distributed to workstations
▫️ Identity-aware gateway integration: Configure AI tools to route through organizational LLM gateway with credentials containing the enrolled user, device, and an allowed client label giving the gateway identity context for routing, policy, and logging.
▫️ Observability: collect session and tool-use activity and attach user, device, and client identity to gateway telemetry for model and token-usage attribution
▫️ Incremental adoption: start with a standalone version, upgrade to a centralized controller-managed mode

 👏 And the best part: it's open source. Come take a look!!

Post summary

Christian Posta announces Agentdesktop, an open-source project intended to manage AI-tool sprawl across employee workstations. The post positions conventional MDM as useful for enrollment, software deployment, and patching, but insufficient for tool-native AI configuration, MCP/skill discovery, sandbox policy, identity-aware gateway use, short-lived runtime credentials, and telemetry. It presents discovery and inventory, reconciliation of supported harness configurations, filesystem/network policy translation, device and user identity, gateway-injected provider credentials, and usage attribution as the intended control layer.

Primary-source quick pass

The post’s project website and public GitHub repository were inspected read-only by direct network access, not by clicking LinkedIn links. At observed repository commit 9204f30f7ba94adac4bd23279c0ba9b5727b3743, the Apache-2.0 project documentation describes discovery/configuration for Claude Code, Claude Desktop, Codex, OpenCode, and VS Code, with sandbox-policy support specifically listed for Claude Code and Codex. Source-visible reconciliation modules map configured writable/denied paths and allowed network domains into those harnesses’ native settings. The published schema says an empty allowed-domain set disables network access and that tool-use input telemetry can include tool arguments. The project also implements OIDC credential acquisition/storage and controller-signed short-lived gateway JWTs; its own README warns that a local asserted client label is useful for policy/attribution but is not cryptographic proof of the calling executable.

Book relevance

  • Candidate chapters: agent governance and desktop control planes; tool execution and sandbox policy; secret distribution and identity-aware gateways; observability and privacy.
  • Candidate claim: endpoint governance for agents must cover the tool-native configuration surface, credential lifecycle, sandbox/egress policy, and observability—not merely device enrollment or software deployment.
  • Candidate example: an endpoint daemon can reconcile a centrally expressed policy into each supported harness’s native filesystem and network configuration while keeping provider keys at a gateway.
  • Counterweight: translating policy into a harness’s native configuration does not itself prove a robust isolation boundary, non-bypassable egress enforcement, safe telemetry handling, or executable-level identity.

Hermione relevance

This is directly relevant to Hermione’s multi-tool desktop/server operation. It reinforces keeping long-lived provider credentials out of agent prompts and local configuration where possible; treating browser, shell, MCP, and skill execution as distinct policy surfaces; using scoped short-lived credentials; and making telemetry opt-in with careful treatment of tool arguments. Before adopting an endpoint-management layer, Hermione should verify its enforcement point, ensure egress rules cannot be bypassed from an agent execution context, keep secrets outside model-visible logs, and test rollback/reconciliation on supported harness versions.

Evidence and limitations

Evidence strength: moderate for the project’s documented and source-visible configuration/credential mechanisms; discovery-only for real-world security, fleet-scale reliability, or governance-effectiveness claims.

posts.title: Self-evolving code review needs governed memory, not just feedback accumulation
posts.headline: I built a self-evolving code review agent!
posts.author: Sumanth P
posts.post_text:
I built a self-evolving code review agent!

Most code review agents use the same prompt every time they run. They can review a diff and generate comments, but they do not remember what your team accepted, rejected, or corrected in previous reviews.

That means the same mistakes can keep showing up across review cycles.

This project adds persistent experiential memory to the review loop.

Before every review, the agent retrieves relevant team rules and similar past review trajectories from memory, then uses that context alongside the current diff to generate review comments.

After the review, the engineer can accept, reject, or edit every comment.

That feedback becomes the learning signal.

Accepted comments reinforce useful rules. Rejected comments create lessons about what should not be flagged. Edited comments refine the team’s preferred convention, scope, or wording.

The agent adapts non-parametrically.

Instead of fine-tuning the underlying model, it improves by storing review outcomes as reusable memory and retrieving the most relevant experience before the next review.

Here is how the loop works:

• Retrieve: search memory for relevant insights and similar past reviews before generating comments
• Review: generate structured feedback using the current diff plus retrieved memory
• Human feedback: pause the workflow and collect an accept, reject, or edit decision for every comment
• Reflect: convert those decisions into reusable natural-language rules with rationale, polarity, scope, and confidence
• Persist: store both the learned insights and complete review trajectory for future retrieval

Over time, the agent builds a memory of how your team actually reviews code without retraining the underlying model.

The full workflow runs locally with LangGraph, Ollama, BGE embeddings, and a vector database for long-term memory.

The interesting part is that every review leaves behind experience that can be retrieved and reused on the next one.

I've shared the complete implementation and setup in the comments!
posts.summary_html:
Post summary

Sumanth P presents a code-review agent that retrieves team rules and past review trajectories before reviewing a supplied change, pauses for an engineer to accept, reject, or edit every generated comment, reflects those decisions into reusable natural-language rules, and persists both insights and trajectories for later retrieval. The claimed adaptation is external-memory based rather than model fine-tuning, with a local stack of LangGraph, Ollama, BGE embeddings, and a vector database.

Primary-source quick pass

The repository named in a captured guest-visible comment was inspected read-only by direct network/Git access, not by clicking in LinkedIn. At commit dc88f37ec43afb29bc3e51db92eb2ee85673323d, the project contains an explicit LangGraph retrieve → review → human-feedback interrupt → reflect → persist graph; two VectorAI collections for insights and trajectories; an Ollama structured-output client; BGE embeddings; and a Streamlit UI that requires one decision per generated comment. Its test covers the graph with fake memory and fake LLM objects. No project dependency, model, database, service, or review workflow was installed or run during this intake.

Book relevance

  • Candidate chapters: agent memory and learning loops; human-in-the-loop systems; coding-agent quality assurance; governance and evaluation of adaptive agents.
  • Candidate claim: persistent operational memory can turn review feedback into a team-specific context layer without changing model weights, but memory is a policy-bearing dataset that needs provenance, retention, retrieval evaluation, and protection from bad feedback.
  • Candidate example: the retrieve/review/feedback/reflect/persist pipeline is a concrete pattern for separating a reversible human decision from later learning and retrieval.
  • Counterweight: a falling rejection rate can indicate alignment with reviewers, not correctness, security coverage, or resistance to overfitting and memory poisoning.

Hermione relevance

This is directly relevant to Hermione's worker and review loops. Feedback and verified outcomes can be stored as scoped, inspectable lessons rather than silently changing a system prompt or model. Before adopting the pattern, Hermione should retain provenance and expiry on each lesson, separate reviewer feedback from authoritative acceptance criteria, scope retrieval by task/repository/risk class, cap retrieved context, evaluate false positives and missed defects, and allow review/rollback of learned rules.

Evidence strength: moderate for the project’s documented and source-visible workflow; discovery-only for claims that it improves review quality, team alignment, or security in real use.

It is a README-style image titled “Self-Evolving Code Review Agent,” showing a local-stack interface and the loop Change → Retrieve → Review → Engineer feedback → Reflect → Persist. posts.title: Agentic API: a stateful gateway above model serving
posts.headline: Agentic API is a stateful API layer that sits in front of vLLM and turns raw model inference into something closer to an agent runtime.
posts.author: Sandhya Ahuja
posts.post_text:
Agentic API is a stateful API layer that sits in front of vLLM and turns raw model inference into something closer to an agent runtime. vLLM is optimized for serving tokens efficiently, but an agent also needs conversation state, tool-call loops, continuation across turns, streaming, and persistence. Agentic API moves that orchestration from the client into the server => a client can continue from a previous_response_id instead of rebuilding and resending the full conversation state, while the gateway restores the session and keeps the loop running.

Tool execution is also explicit => gateway-owned tools such as web search and MCP tools can run server-side, client-owned tools such as Codex shell or editor actions are returned to the client, and provider-owned tools pass through to the model backend. That separation matters because it gives open models served by vLLM a stateful, OpenAI-compatible agent interface without forcing every application to implement its own persistence and tool orchestration layer.

GitHub Repo: https://lnkd.in/gamTQ9PX
posts.summary_html:

It describes an ownership split in which gateway tools run on the server, client tools remain with the client, and provider tools pass to the backend.

The guest-visible post exposed the lnkd.in/gamTQ9PX repository shortlink. It was resolved by a normal network fetch, not clicked through LinkedIn, to https://github.com/vllm-project/agentic-api. posts.title: Code as Agent Harness: executable state and verification, not merely code generation
posts.headline: Code as Agent Harness!
posts.author: Sumanth P
posts.post_text:
Code as Agent Harness!

Code is no longer just something AI agents generate. It is increasingly becoming the execution layer through which they reason, act, manage state, use tools, and verify their own work.

That distinction matters.

A model can decide what it wants to do, but long-running agents still need a structured way to turn those decisions into actions. They need to call tools, execute code, preserve intermediate state, inspect results, recover from failures, and coordinate work across multiple steps.

The paper frames code itself as that harness.

Instead of treating planning, memory, tool use, and execution as separate pieces of infrastructure, code becomes the common interface connecting the model to all of them.

The paper breaks this into three layers:

• Harness interface: code connects the agent to reasoning, actions, and the environment it is operating in

• Harness mechanisms: planning, memory, tool use, execution feedback, and optimization keep long-running tasks reliable

• Multi-agent harness: shared code artifacts become a way for multiple agents to coordinate, review each other's work, and verify results

This applies well beyond coding agents.

The paper covers GUI and OS automation, scientific discovery, embodied agents, DevOps, personalization, enterprise workflows, and other systems where agents need to interact with an environment rather than simply generate text.

The interesting part is how this changes the role of code in AI systems.

Code used to be primarily an output of the model. Now it can also represent the agent's plan, tools, state, interaction with the environment, and even the mechanism used to verify whether an action actually worked.

That makes harness engineering a much bigger part of building reliable agents than simply wrapping an LLM with a few tool calls.

I've shared the paper in the comments!
posts.summary_html:
Post summary

Sumanth P frames code as the operational harness of an AI agent: the interface through which a model turns decisions into tool calls, state, execution, feedback, recovery, and verification. The post organizes the idea into a harness interface, harness mechanisms, and multi-agent harnesses, and applies it to coding, GUI/OS automation, scientific work, DevOps, and enterprise workflows. It points to the paper Code as Agent Harness in a visible comment.

Primary-source quick pass

The paper URL appearing in a guest-visible LinkedIn comment was fetched directly from arXiv, not clicked through LinkedIn: https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.18747v1 (submitted 18 May 2026). Its abstract describes the same three-layer survey: code connecting reasoning/action/environment modeling; mechanisms such as planning, memory, tool use, and feedback-driven control; and multi-agent coordination, review, and verification through shared code artifacts. It explicitly names unresolved issues including evaluation beyond final task success, incomplete-feedback verification, regression-free improvement, consistent shared state, and human oversight for safety-critical actions.

This confirms the existence and high-level scope of the cited preprint, not that any particular harness implementation is reliable, secure, or production-ready. A Semantic Scholar query was rate-limited, so no citation-based impact claim is made.

Book relevance

  • Candidate chapters: agent orchestration; durable execution and state; verification and recoverability; multi-agent governance.
  • Candidate claim: reliable agents need executable, inspectable artifacts that connect plans to bounded actions, explicit state, feedback, and verification—not only an LLM plus tool calls.
  • Candidate example: a runbook, task ledger, reviewed diff, progress JSON, or reproducible command can serve as a shared contract between an executor and an independent verifier.
  • Counterweight: shared code alone does not establish correctness. Fixed environments, scoped authority, deterministic checks, provenance, and actual reviewer execution are required before one agent can trust another's reported result.

Hermione relevance

This is highly relevant to Hermione. Her worker profiles, queue checkpoints, sanitized artifacts, bounded retries, explicit terminal transitions, and post-action verification are concrete harness mechanisms. The practical improvement is to preserve the distinction between a model's plan and a verified state change: each side effect should have a durable checkpoint, an explicit authority boundary, a test or read-back, and a recoverable path. Shared artifacts should be reviewable and minimal rather than a channel for untrusted instructions.

Evidence and limitations

Evidence strength: moderate for the cited arXiv preprint's existence and stated conceptual framework; discovery-only for LinkedIn engagement and for real-world reliability, safety, productivity, or generality claims. No implementation, benchmark, installation, or agent workflow was run.

  • The submitted lnkd.in URL resolved through one normal non-interactive HTTP redirect to a referral-bearing LinkedIn share URL. The archive and catalogue use the sanitized canonical activity URL. No CAPTCHA was presented, interacted with, or bypassed.
  • Nine comments embedded in guest-visible metadata were captured. Their substantive theme is that shared artifacts need reproducible environments, governance, permissions, auditability, and independent verification. They are social discussion rather than independent validation; no comment, reply, sorting control, or truncated text was opened.
  • The authenticated viewport visibly showed the target post and no login wall, MFA, CAPTCHA, or security checkpoint. It also displayed a pre-existing messaging overlay, so raw authenticated text, metadata, and screenshot remain local-only and are not committed or used beyond target verification.
  • One image reproduces a paper page/diagram attributed to Illinois, Meta, and Stanford. It depicts agent-to-code-to-environment feedback and execution/verification, the three harness layers, and application domains. It contains no quantitative performance claim.

Media summary

One static image is a paper-style overview titled Code as Agent Harness (arXiv:2605.18747v1; image-side date 18 May 2026). It visually presents code as an inspectable, executable, stateful bridge between an agent and its external environment, with feedback and verification. It is illustrative source material, not an experimental result.
