posts.title: LinkedIn intake summary
posts.headline: Turn your entire codebase into a queryable knowledge graph!
posts.author: Sumanth P
posts.post_text:
Turn your entire codebase into a queryable knowledge graph!

Graphify is an AI coding assistant skill that maps your entire project into a knowledge graph you can query. Works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, and 20+ more coding agents.

Type "/graphify ." and it processes everything in your project. Code across 36 languages, SQL schemas, shell scripts, docs, PDFs, images, and videos, all mapped into one graph. Processing happens locally, no API needed for code.

The output is three files. An interactive HTML visualization you can open in a browser. A Markdown report with key concepts, surprising connections, and suggested questions. And a JSON graph you can query directly.

Instead of grepping through files or hoping your AI finds the right context, you query the graph. "What connects auth to the database?" "Find the path between UserService and DatabasePool." The graph answers precisely because it has the full picture, not just what's in the context window.

Builds a Git hook for auto-rebuild on every commit so the graph stays current as the codebase changes. Pushes to Neo4j for team sharing via MCP server. Generates a PR dashboard showing graph impact before merge.

Key capabilities:

• Maps code, docs, PDFs, images, and videos into one knowledge graph
• 36 languages via tree-sitter, processed locally
• Works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, and 20+ agents
• Query the graph instead of grepping through files
• Auto-rebuild on commit via Git hook
• Neo4j and FalkorDB integration for team sharing
• PR dashboard with graph impact analysis

100% open source.

I've shared the link in the replies!
posts.summary_html:
Content assessment

The post describes Graphify as a coding-assistant skill that maps code, schemas, scripts, documents, PDFs, images, and videos into a queryable knowledge graph. Claimed outputs include HTML visualization, Markdown analysis, JSON graph data, Git-hook freshness, Neo4j/FalkorDB sharing, MCP access, and PR impact analysis.

The durable issue is not whether a graph looks impressive. It is whether every edge exposes provenance, extraction method, confidence/ambiguity, source span, parser coverage, and freshness. Without those, agents can mistake regex/name matching or semantic inference for parser-confirmed architecture.

Primary-source check

The repository linked in the author's visible comment exists and was checked directly by network fetch rather than clicking LinkedIn. GitHub reported a public Python repository under MIT, latest release v0.9.12 published 2026-07-10, approximately 82,224 stars and 8,091 forks at inspection time. The README documents tree-sitter/AST extraction, graph/query artifacts, incremental updates, a post-commit hook, MCP/Neo4j options, and EXTRACTED/INFERRED/AMBIGUOUS edge labels.

Important qualification: local deterministic processing applies to code. The README says documents, PDFs, images, and video can use Claude or a configured API/model for semantic extraction, so “no API needed” should not be generalized to all inputs. Recent release notes document fixes for false cross-language edges, ambiguous Java resolution, dangling edges, missing optional extractors, and non-deterministic merges—evidence that graph correctness remains an active engineering boundary.

Book relevance

High (9/10). Candidate placement:

  • confidence-aware repository context for coding agents;
  • static analysis, knowledge graphs, and context engineering;
  • freshness and provenance in generated knowledge;
  • token reduction versus correctness and measured outcomes;
  • privacy boundaries in local/hybrid multimodal extraction.

Candidate claim/example: repository graphs can reduce blind searching and preserve structural context, but they become trustworthy agent infrastructure only when confirmed, inferred, and ambiguous edges remain distinguishable and freshness/coverage are measurable.

Hermione relevance

High (9/10). Graphify could help Hermione navigate unfamiliar repositories, inspect dependencies, identify high-connectivity nodes, and provide structured context to workers. It should not replace direct code inspection, search, tests, or parser-specific tools.

Suggested improvement: evaluate Graphify on a representative polyglot repository, pin the version, inspect exported provenance/source spans, benchmark full and incremental rebuilds, audit secret/model/API data flow, and require low-confidence edges to trigger verification rather than edits.

Evidence caveats

Evidence is moderate for project existence/features documented in primary sources, discovery-only for effectiveness claims. Exact 36-language/20+-agent coverage, privacy across all input types, rebuild performance, PR-dashboard behavior, edge accuracy, and the project-published 71.5× token benchmark were not independently tested. Star count establishes attention, not correctness. See wider-web-research.md for the primary-source findings and recommended evaluation.

posts.title: LinkedIn intake summary
posts.headline: GPT-5.6-Sol deleted 74,000 lines of code and made my app better (after 47 hours of work)
posts.author: Peter Gostev
posts.post_text:
GPT-5.6-Sol deleted 74,000 lines of code and made my app better (after 47 hours of work)

I have a slop-coded app that I need for work - it pulls in the data, it helps me create visuals, just a local app for me. Somehow, feature after feature, it grew to gigantic 105,704 lines of code. With every new model, I tried to re-build it autonomously and it never worked - goes round in circles, no visual or feature parity etc complete waste of time.

When testing GPT-5.6-Sol, gave a pretty ambitious task of rebuilding the app with the new architecture, while reducing the lines of code by 70% and test time by 75%.

I set a /goal, let it run for over 2 full days (47 hours) with minimal checking or guidance from my side.

I was pretty sceptical and a little nervous to finally try it and holy crap - it actually worked!

 Not only it worked, but it was actually better - snappier, less buggy, while maintaining full visual and feature parity. Looking at the architecture too, it became a lot simpler, fewer random add-ons or ad-hoc decisions.

After the rebuild, I did introduce few rules for my projects so agents have to adhere to existing architecture and do only minimal changes when implementing new features.

This makes me less worried about the slopware we might be producing now, better models CAN actually fix it.
posts.summary_html:
Claim and assessment

The author says a local, feature-accumulated application had grown to 105,704 production-and-test lines. GPT-5.6-Sol was given a /goal to rebuild it with a new architecture while reducing lines of code and test time, then ran for roughly 47 hours with minimal human checking. The author reports a rebuilt app with full feature/visual parity, fewer bugs, greater responsiveness, and simpler architecture.

The accompanying image claims:

  • Production + test LOC: 105,704 → 31,711 (70.00% lower; 73,993 fewer lines)
  • Deterministic test time: 96.72s → 8.50s (91.21% faster)
  • Controls validated: 954/954 (100%)
  • Visual parity checks: 42/42 pixel-identical (100%)
  • Total tracked execution time: 47.21 hours

The most durable point is not deletion volume. It is that large autonomous rewrites need explicit outcome criteria, regression tests, visual parity checks, architecture constraints, minimal-change rules, and reviewable before/after evidence. Fewer lines may reflect removed duplication and complexity, but line count alone is not a quality metric.

Book relevance

High (9/10). Candidate placement:

  • autonomous software maintenance and large-scale agentic rewrites;
  • acceptance criteria, regression gates, and visual verification;
  • technical-debt remediation and architecture governance;
  • long-running agent loops and observability;
  • why dramatic social coding claims require reproducible evidence.

Candidate example: a reported 47-hour autonomous rebuild illustrates how measurable gates can bound an ambitious agent task, while also showing why LOC reduction and author-reported parity are insufficient without repository, commit, test, cost, and independent-review evidence.

Hermione relevance

High (9/10). Hermione should not treat “the agent finished” or “fewer lines” as success. For long-running code work, she should require a baseline and target, preserve the original, run independent tests, inspect diffs, use visual checks where relevant, record cost/tokens/time, and obtain reviewer approval before replacement or deployment.

Suggested improvement: formalize rewrite/refactor gates in delegated coding workflows—branch isolation, rollback, test and performance baselines, architecture invariants, security/dependency review, independent verification, and explicit human approval for large destructive diffs.

Evidence caveats

Evidence strength is discovery-only. No repository, commit diff, test suite, screenshots, benchmark harness, token/cost record, architecture comparison, security/dependency analysis, or independent reproduction was provided or inspected. The model name and capabilities are author claims in this intake. “Less buggy,” “snappier,” feature parity, and visual parity are not independently verified. A successful rewrite may also remove behavior that tests do not cover. Only 10 of 35 reported comments were archived.

posts.title: LinkedIn intake summary
posts.headline: Last month, Google released a new knowledge spec called the Open Knowledge Format (OKF).
posts.author: Martin-Jan Sklorz
posts.post_text:
Last month, Google released a new knowledge spec called the Open Knowledge Format (OKF).

It’s incredibly simple: just Markdown files with some YAML metadata; linked together like a wiki. No SDKs, no proprietary software and no special runtime required.

It might sound underwhelming, but that seems to be the goal.

Right now, building AI agents is difficult because context is scattered. Information about data schemas, metrics and business logic is buried in code comments, Confluence or just in people's heads. Because this information is so fragmented, every team has to build its own way to connect it, often getting locked into specific tools.

OKF's approach is different. Instead of another complex service, it provides a format. These files live in your Git repository right next to your code. Humans can read them in any editor and AI agents can parse them directly without needing a middleman. You write the information once and any agent can use it, too.

To be clear: a format doesn't solve everything. Markdown files in a repo won't stay accurate on their own; you still need the discipline to review and update them. But OKF removes the technical excuse for not documenting your knowledge.

When your agent answers wrong, do you know which file to fix, or is that knowledge still living in someone's head?
posts.summary_html:
Content assessment

The post presents OKF as Markdown files with YAML metadata, linked like a wiki and stored beside code in Git. Its intended benefit is portable, human-readable knowledge about schemas, metrics, and business logic that agents can consume without a proprietary service or runtime. The post correctly preserves the central operational caveat: a format does not maintain itself; review and update discipline are still required.

Book relevance

High (9/10). Candidate placement:

  • context engineering and organizational memory for agents;
  • repository-native knowledge and provenance;
  • open formats versus proprietary knowledge middleware;
  • documentation freshness, governance, and human-agent interoperability;
  • MCP/tool access compared with knowledge/context access.

Candidate claim/example: plain, version-controlled knowledge artifacts can reduce context fragmentation and make agent errors more repairable by providing an identifiable file to update—but only when ownership, review, validation, and freshness mechanisms are present.

Hermione relevance

High (9/10). Hermione already relies on repo-local instructions, skills, catalogues, and project context. OKF's framing supports a portable knowledge layer that both humans and agents can inspect and version. The useful change is not merely creating more Markdown: knowledge entries should have owners, source/provenance, review dates, validation, and links to the workflows that consume them.

Suggested improvement: evaluate OKF against existing Hermes skills, AGENTS.md/CLAUDE.md, memories, source registries, and catalogues; prototype only where it improves portability, traceability, and repairability without duplicating stale context.

Evidence caveats

Evidence strength is discovery-only. posts.headline: 14x faster and 90% cheaper LLM inference.
posts.author: Akshay Pachaar
posts.post_text:
14x faster and 90% cheaper LLM inference.

(100% open-source, KV cache management)

LMCache is an open-source KV cache management layer that plugs into vLLM, SGLang, and TensorRT-LLM.

Here's how it works:

LLMs recompute their understanding of the same content on every request. The same system prompts, the same documents, processed from scratch every time, and a single GPU throws away roughly 15 TB of this reusable cache per day.

LMCache stores that cache and serves it back on repeat requests, running as a separate process completely outside the inference engine.

The engine just asks for the cache blocks it needs. LMCache handles all the heavy data movement across GPU, CPU, disk, and remote storage in parallel, so cache work never steals compute from inference.

It also reuses cache beyond exact prefixes. Their CacheBlend technique (EuroSys 2025 Best Paper) keeps RAG documents cached no matter what order they appear in.

On H200s with a 235B model, that adds up to 14x faster time-to-first-token and 4x faster decoding. And since reuse skips the compute entirely (the same reason providers discount cached tokens by 90%), the cost savings follow directly.

The repo has the full architecture breakdown, benchmarks, and a Kubernetes operator for production use.

I just shipped an open-source agent skill that turns your coding agent into a Meta LOOP 🤯

Claude Fable 5 as the advisor. GPT-5.6 as the orchestrator. Gemini 3.5 Flash as the worker.

Installs in 10 seconds with one command. 100% open source.

GPT-5.6 orchestrates. It splits your task into self-contained briefs, dispatches them, and verifies every result that comes back.

Gemini 3.5 Flash runs the workers. Up to 20 in parallel, each one stateless, each seeing only its own brief.

Claude Fable 5 advises. Consulted exactly twice, before work starts and before it ships. It critiques. It never executes.

The economics are the point. Cheap parallel generation where volume wins, expensive judgment only where it changes a decision.

Multi-model loops usually die three ways: context leaks, silent partial failures, judgment applied too late. Each one has a rule here.

Every brief carries its full inputs and acceptance criteria inline, so no worker depends on another. Every result gets judged against its own criteria and either passes, gets redispatched with the named failure, or escalates. Every advisor note gets applied or explicitly rebutted before anything ships.

Budgets are hard-capped. 20 worker calls, 5 advisor consults. A run can't quietly burn a hole in your API bill.

Give it an ambitious goal and walk away. You come back to a verified deliverable with a full per-subtask ledger.

posts.title: LinkedIn intake summary — Agentic code isolation architectures
posts.headline: Isolating Agentic Code: A Guide to Infrastructure for AI Agents | Ajay Singh posted on the topic | LinkedIn
posts.author: Ajay Singh
posts.post_text:
Everyone is talking about AI agents writing code. Far fewer are talking about the infrastructure required when they actually execute it.

If you give an LLM an autonomous execution environment, standard containerization is no longer enough. Agentic code is non-deterministic and inherently untrusted.

If you are building agentic workflows, here is a breakdown of the isolation tooling landscape—and exactly when to use (or avoid) each approach:

1. MicroVMs (Hardware-Level Isolation)
The Tools: E2B, AWS Firecracker.
MicroVMs boot their own kernel in ~150ms. If an agent executes a kernel exploit, it only crashes its own isolated instance.
✅ When to use: Ephemeral, high-throughput agent execution. Perfect for multi-step task loops where you need fast, highly isolated environments that destroy themselves immediately after the run.
❌ When NOT to use: If your agent requires massive, persistent workspaces across weeks, or if you need heavy GPU-accelerated workloads (unless you are prepared to manage complex self-hosted PCIe passthrough).

2. Userspace Kernels & Persistent Workspaces
The Tools: Daytona, Northflank, Agent Sandbox (gVisor).
These tools intercept system calls before they hit the host kernel, or manage persistent, stateful pods that can pause and resume.
✅ When to use: "Dev-in-a-box" agents. Use this if your agent needs to maintain state across a massive repository, install dependencies over multiple turns, and retain its environment over days.
❌ When NOT to use: When your primary risk is bare-metal performance. Abstraction layers like gVisor add overhead and can limit raw hardware capabilities.

3. Standard Containers
The Tools: Default Docker.
✅ When to use: Local development, testing your orchestration framework, or running fully trusted, static scripts.
❌ When NOT to use: Production. Containers share the host kernel. Giving an autonomous agent root inside a standard container is a direct path to a sandbox escape.

The Golden Rule:
Layer 1 isolation (the sandbox) is just the start. You still need Layer 2 guardrails: default-deny network egress, short-lived ephemeral credentials, and hard compute timeouts.

2. Userspace Kernels & Persistent Workspaces The Tools: Daytona, Northflank, Agent Sandbox (gVisor). These tools intercept system calls before they hit the host kernel, or manage persistent, stateful pods that can pause and resume. ✅ When to use: "Dev-in-a-box" agents. Use this if your agent needs to maintain state across a massive repository, install dependencies over multiple turns, and retain its environment over days. ❌ When NOT to use: When your primary risk is bare-metal performance. Abstraction layers like gVisor add overhead and can limit raw hardware capabilities.

3. Standard Containers The Tools: Default Docker. ✅ When to use: Local development, testing your orchestration framework, or running fully trusted, static scripts. ❌ When NOT to use: Production. Containers share the host kernel. Giving an autonomous agent root inside a standard container is a direct path to a sandbox escape.

The Golden Rule: Layer 1 isolation (the sandbox) is just the start. You still need Layer 2 guardrails: default-deny network egress, short-lived ephemeral credentials, and hard compute timeouts.

#AgenticAI #Sandboxing #SoftwareEngineering #AIArchitecture #CyberSecurity

Media summary

Single 800x436 JPEG diagram titled 'AGENTIC CODING ISOLATION (ACI) ARCHITECTURES: MicroVM, Sandbox, Container'. It compares MicroVM isolation (e.g., Firecracker) with dedicated kernel/hardware virtualization, strongest isolation, high resource overhead, negligible escape risk; sandbox isolation (e.g., gVisor) using userspace kernel/syscall interception, high isolation, medium overhead, very low escape risk; and container isolation (e.g., Docker) where app containers share the host kernel, weak isolation for untrusted code, minimal overhead, high escape risk. The diagram labels Docker as not for agentic execution of untrusted code.

Book relevance

Very high. This post gives a concise taxonomy for agent runtime isolation: microVMs for ephemeral high-throughput untrusted execution, userspace-kernel/persistent workspaces for stateful dev-in-a-box agents, and plain containers only for trusted/local/testing contexts. It fits chapters on agent runtime security, sandboxing, AI coding agents, infrastructure choices, secrets/egress governance, and recovery semantics.

Hermione relevance

Very high. Hermione-like agents execute shell commands, run code, use browsers, process web/social inputs, and may delegate tasks across worker profiles. The durable lesson is directly operational: standard containers are not enough for untrusted autonomous code; isolation must be paired with default-deny network egress, short-lived credentials, hard timeouts, and disposable/revertible workspaces.

Potential Hermione improvement: use this post as a runtime-security checklist for future agent execution environments: choose microVM/gVisor/persistent workspace intentionally by task risk, keep secrets outside model/tool context, enforce egress outside the guest where possible, set timeouts/quotas, and preserve rollback/audit trails.

Evidence strength

Discovery-only / moderate. The taxonomy is technically plausible and aligns with common security framing, but the exact claims such as ~150ms microVM boot time, escape-risk labels, and tool fit should be corroborated against primary docs and security evidence for Firecracker, E2B, Daytona, Northflank, gVisor, Docker, and related sandbox systems.

Limitations

  • Safe LinkedIn intake only; no LinkedIn links/buttons were clicked.
  • No external/runtime-security primary sources were inspected during this intake.
  • No comments were exposed/captured, so discussion-derived due diligence is absent.
  • Social post is discovery evidence, not independent validation of isolation guarantees or escape-risk levels.

posts.title: LinkedIn intake summary — Omnigent / meta-harness for AI coding agents
posts.headline: The meta-harness for all your AI coding agents!
posts.author: Sumanth P
posts.post_text:
The meta-harness for all your AI coding agents!

Omnigent is an open-source orchestration layer that sits above your AI coding agents. Orchestrates Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Hermes, and Pi through a single interface. Swap or combine harnesses without rewriting anything.

The problem with using multiple coding agents: each lives in its own terminal, has its own setup, its own commands. When you want to switch or combine them, you start over. Omnigent removes that. One layer above all of them, consistent interface regardless of which agent is running underneath.

Sessions follow you across devices. Start in your terminal, continue in the browser, pick it up on your phone. Messages, sub-agents, terminals, and files stay in sync across every surface.

Multi-agent orchestration works within a single session. Point one agent at another's work. Delegate tasks in parallel across Claude Code, Codex, and Pi running in separate git worktrees, then route the diffs to a reviewer from a different vendor. All from one session.

Policy enforcement runs at three levels: server, agent, and session. Approve before shell commands execute, cap spend, limit tool calls. Stacks consistently across every harness you plug in.

Custom agents via YAML. Define your own with tools, MCP servers, and sub-agents. Two ship out of the box: Polly, a multi-agent coding orchestrator, and Debby, a dual-head Claude and GPT brainstorming agent.

Key capabilities:

• Orchestrates Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Hermes, Pi, and custom agents
• Sessions follow you across terminal, browser, and phone
• Multi-agent collaboration within a single session
• Policy enforcement at server, agent, and session level
• Cloud sandboxes via Modal, Daytona, E2B, and Kubernetes
• Custom agents defined in YAML with tools and MCP servers
• Real-time team collaboration and session sharing

100% open source.

I've shared the link in the replies!

posts.title: LinkedIn intake summary — OpenWiki / coding-agent context engineering
posts.headline: Auto-generated codebase docs rot as code changes, and a wiki nobody maintains feeds wrong context to your coding agent.
posts.author: André Lindenberg
posts.post_text:
Auto-generated codebase docs rot as code changes, and a wiki nobody maintains feeds wrong context to your coding agent. OpenWiki generates a repo wiki, then a CI workflow regenerates it from diffs and opens a PR to keep it current. Pointers into AGENTS·md and CLAUDE·md mean the agent reads accurate context instead of re-exploring the repo every task, so fewer edits land on wrong assumptions. 7.3k stars, MIT.
#CodingAgents #ContextEngineering #DevEx

posts.title: LinkedIn intake summary: CubeSandbox / AI-agent runtime security
posts.headline: When an agent runs untrusted code, isolating it is the easy part.
posts.author: André Lindenberg
posts.post_text:
When an agent runs untrusted code, isolating it is the easy part. Recovering from what it did is the hard part. CubeSandbox gives each agent a hardware-isolated microVM with copy-on-write snapshots, instant clone, and rollback to any prior state, plus a credential vault that keeps keys out of the model context and egress audit logs. E2B-SDK compatible. 7.6k stars, Apache-2.0.
#AIAgents #RuntimeSecurity #AgentInfra #OpenSource
posts.summary_html:

posts.title: LinkedIn intake summary — PixelRAG / screenshots for RAG
posts.headline: STOP PARSING HTML FOR RAG.
posts.author: Charly Wargnier
posts.post_text:
STOP PARSING HTML FOR RAG. JUST SCREENSHOT IT 🔥

Researchers from UC Berkeley just released PixelRAG, an open-source system that skips HTML parsing entirely.

Why is it changing web scraping for good?

Well, instead of scraping a page into text and embedding chunks:

#1 it screenshots that page and retrieves the image
#2 a vision-language model then reads the answer straight off the pixels

This solves a real problem: parsing is where RAG quietly loses context:
→ A single HTML-to-text parser can drop 40%+ of a page
→ Tables, charts, and complex layouts get flattened or deleted
→ Changing parsers alone can swing accuracy by 10 points

By indexing the page exactly as a human sees it, PixelRAG beats the strongest text RAG baseline by 18.1% on text-only QA.

To prove it scales, the team built a visual index of all 8.28M Wikipedia articles using 30M+ screenshots.

It even includes a Claude Code plugin (pixelbrowse) that gives Claude native "eyes" to read live pages locally, how cool is that?

100% free and open-source (Apache-2.0).

Here's the repo → https://lnkd.in/erUuKhyc

BONUS: If you’re building retrieval systems, my friend Akshay Pachaar recently wrote a great guide on X about slashing your RAG corpus by 40x and tokens by 3x.

Check it out → https://lnkd.in/erdrYzBW
posts.summary_html:

The post claims parser choice and HTML-to-text conversion can lose substantial page signal, especially tables/charts/layout, and says PixelRAG beats a strong text RAG baseline by 18.1% on text-only QA while scaling to all 8.28M Wikipedia articles via 30M+ screenshots.

posts.title: The entire RAG industry is about to get cooked.
posts.headline: The entire RAG industry is about to get cooked.
posts.author: Basia Kubicka
posts.post_text:
The entire RAG industry is about to get cooked.

Researchers built a new RAG approach that:

- runs without a vector database.
- skips embeddings entirely.
- never chunks the source document.
- ignores similarity search completely.

And it just scored 98.7% on long, complex financial filings
(~99 of 100 questions answered correctly)
vs 31% for GPT-4o with search - on the same long filings.

Yes, "vectorless RAG" is a real thing. I checked.

I've been testing RAG stacks for months.
Vector retrieval, hybrid, the works.

Most of them fall apart on long documents.

And PageIndex is the first one that made me rethink chunking entirely.
It's open-source, free, and built by VectifyAI: https://lnkd.in/ezA_pkHv

Here's what you need to know
1️⃣ The architecture - tree index, not vector index
↳ It generates a Table-of-Contents tree of any PDF
↳ A Tree Navigator Agent reasons through that tree, like AlphaGo's tree search
↳ Retrieval returns page and section references, not opaque vector hits

2️⃣ Why it beats chunked vector RAG
↳ Similarity is not the same as relevance for legal, finance, and technical docs
↳ 98.7% on FinanceBench vs 31% for GPT-4o with search - on the same long filings
↳ Every retrieval is traceable. No more "vibe retrieval."

3️⃣ What you don't have to run anymore
↳ No vector database to host, no embeddings to re-run when docs change
↳ It carries conversation context across turns, so follow-ups stay grounded
↳ Simpler stack, lower cost, less to maintain

4️⃣ How to try it today
↳ Install with pip3 and run python3 run_pageindex.py with your PDF path
↳ Open their Colab notebook for a minimal vectorless RAG demo on your own document
↳ Fork the agentic example (OpenAI Agents SDK) and swap a vector tool for a tree tool

Vector RAG isn't dead.

But for long professional documents where similarity fails,
this is the architecture I'd reach for first.

My vector database took the news poorly.
(We're working through it.)

What's the use case where similarity search failed you?
Drop a comment below.

♻️ Repost to help the builders in your network.
And follow Basia Kubicka for more on building with AI.

📷 Thank you, Rakesh Gohel, for a great infographic! Give him a follow!
